summaries.example: Imagine two labels: “triangle” and “a shape with three to five sides, with sides that are not too different in length.” Both might pick out some shapes, but “triangle” seems to describe a clearer pattern. Philosophers use this kind of comparison to ask whether one property fits the world better or is less oddly pieced together.
summaries.summary: The entry explains a special philosophical meaning of “natural.” A natural property is not simply a property found in nature, and an unnatural property is not necessarily made by humans. Instead, philosophers who accept naturalness think some properties fit the world's structure better than others. Being a triangle may seem more natural than having a complicated shape described by several limits. Being green may seem more natural than being “green before a chosen time or blue afterward.” Naturalness can come in degrees, and some theories say that perfectly natural properties are the basic building blocks of reality. If we knew which things had all of these basic properties, we might have a complete description of the world. The idea has also been connected with what makes things similar, how scientific laws work, how words get their meanings, and which patterns are reasonable to learn from. The entry also explains that philosophers disagree. Some think naturalness is useful and objective. Others think different jobs, such as explaining similarity and explaining language, may not all point to one single ranking of properties. The concept may also be vague. So naturalness is a useful but debated idea in metaphysics, the part of philosophy that studies reality and what it is made of.
key_ideas: Naturalness, in this philosophical use, is not about whether people made something or whether it occurs outdoors.
Philosophers often think naturalness comes in degrees: some properties can be more natural than others.
Some philosophers think perfectly natural properties would give a complete description of reality.
Other philosophers doubt that naturalness names one clear, objective feature of the world.
The idea has been used to think about similarity, scientific laws, language, and good reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea of natural properties asks whether the world itself has better and worse ways of being divided into kinds. That question affects science, language, similarity, and learning from evidence. It also reminds us to separate a useful pattern from a rule that merely reflects our temporary interests. At the same time, the disagreements show why philosophers should be careful before treating a familiar word as if it had one simple meaning.

important_terms.definition: A feature that something can have, such as being green, heavy, or triangular.
The philosophical idea that some properties match the world's structure better than others.
A property at the highest level of naturalness in a theory; it is sometimes called fundamental.
A property made by combining ideas in a complicated or unusual way, such as “green before a certain time or blue afterward.”

questions_to_think_about: Is “green” a better pattern than a rule that changes after a special date? Why?
Could a property be natural even if people cannot change anything that has it?
Would knowing the most basic properties be enough to describe everything?
Do words usually point more easily to simple patterns than to complicated ones?

summaries.example: Consider the properties green and grue. “Green” applies to things that are green, while “grue” applies to things green before a selected time and blue afterward. The two properties may match all observations made so far, yet many philosophers regard green as more natural. This contrast raises a problem for induction: evidence about emeralds can support “all emeralds are green” without supporting the corresponding grue-generalization to the same degree. The source stresses, however, that the connection between naturalness and projectibility is a proposal, not an established solution.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a technical metaphysical use of “natural.” On this use, properties such as being triangular, being electrically charged, or being green may be more natural than properties constructed by arbitrary restrictions or time-dependent combinations. The contrast is not between human-made and non-human-made features. A highly unnatural property can be entirely outside human control, and many philosophers regard naturalness as objective: its ordering would remain even if our interests, practices, or perhaps intelligent life had been different. Naturalness is generally understood as graded, with a maximum level called perfect naturalness or fundamentality. Lewis’s influential picture treats fundamental properties as an exhaustive and non-redundant basis for the world. A related proposal defines relative naturalness through the simplicity of definitions in terms of perfectly natural properties, although this proposal faces problems involving infinite definitions and fine-grained differences between properties. The entry surveys applications. Natural properties may make for similarity and help define duplication or intrinsicness. They may determine what is true across possible worlds, contribute to theories of laws of nature, and act as “reference magnets,” making them easier, other things equal, for language users and thinkers to refer to. Naturalness has also been connected with induction: greenness may be more projectible than grueness, though the exact connection is disputed. The entry discusses extensions to classes, pluralities, propositions, concepts, higher-order predicates, magnitudes, and natural kinds, while emphasizing that these extensions raise separate problems. key_ideas: Naturalness is intended as an objective distinction: it should not depend merely on human interests, vocabulary, or practices, though the idea is controversial.
Naturalness is usually treated as graded, with a possible maximal level of perfect naturalness or fundamentality.
Lewis connects perfect naturalness with a complete and non-redundant basis for reality; other philosophers propose different accounts.
Naturalness has been related to similarity, duplication, intrinsicness, modality, laws of nature, meaning, induction, and epistemic value.
The source distinguishes natural properties from natural kinds, magnitudes, classes, propositions, and concepts; whether the same notion applies to each is unsettled.
Critics argue that the various roles assigned to naturalness may not be jointly satisfied by one ranking, and that “natural” may be vague.
summaries.why_it_matters: Naturalness is proposed as a bridge between metaphysics and other areas of philosophy. If some properties are fundamental, they might explain why certain similarities matter, why some descriptions are simpler, how laws are selected, and why some concepts are easier to use or project from evidence. But the proposal also carries significant commitments about properties, possible worlds, definitions, and the structure of reality. Studying the objections helps clarify whether these different explanatory jobs really belong to one notion or should be separated.

important_terms.definition: A feature, relation, or other property-like item that can be instantiated by things or tuples of things.
A debated, objective-seeming ranking of properties, according to which some are less arbitrary or more world-structuring than others.
A property that is not outranked by any other property in naturalness; Lewis also calls such properties fundamental.
A property whose instances are picked out by an especially complicated or arbitrary combination, often illustrated by “grue.”
A relation in which two things match with respect to their intrinsic, perfectly natural features and relations.
The idea that facts about less fundamental properties depend on facts about more fundamental ones, without changing those underlying facts.
A proposal that truths about the distribution of perfectly natural properties determine all truths across possible worlds.
The idea that a hypothesis or property is suitable for generalization from evidence; philosophers have linked this to simplicity and naturalness.

questions_to_think_about: If two properties are necessarily coextensive, must they have the same naturalness?
Could physics identify perfectly natural properties, or would that require philosophical assumptions beyond physics?
Should naturalness explain which scientific generalizations are projectible, or should projectibility be explained independently?
Can a complete description of reality be stated using only fundamental properties and the objects that instantiate them?
If different theories use “naturalness” for incompatible purposes, are they disagreeing about reality or about a theoretical term?

summaries.example: Suppose a class is called “things that are blue on Mondays and red on other days.” It may be easy to describe, but it seems less like a basic pattern than “being blue” or “being red.” Philosophers might call the first property gerrymandered. They can then ask whether this difference is truly in the world or is only a result of what people find useful to notice.
summaries.summary: The entry studies the philosophical idea that some properties are more natural than others. Here, “natural” does not mean occurring outdoors, untouched by people, or easy for humans to control. A property can be unnatural in this technical sense even when humans have no power over it. Instead, naturalness is meant to describe how well a property fits the structure of reality. Being a triangle may seem more natural than a complicated shape defined by several limits. Being green may seem more natural than being green before a chosen time and blue afterward. Such unusual combinations are often called gerrymandered. Many philosophers think naturalness has degrees. At the top may be perfectly natural, or fundamental, properties. On one influential view, a full description of the world would say which objects have each fundamental property and which objects stand in each fundamental relation. Philosophers disagree about how to identify these properties and whether physics alone could do so. Naturalness has several proposed uses. It may help explain similarity, duplication, intrinsic properties, scientific laws, the meanings of words, and why some patterns are better supported by evidence. The entry also considers whether naturalness applies to classes, groups of things, propositions, concepts, quantities such as mass, and natural kinds. These extensions are not automatic. A major disagreement concerns whether all these uses can be explained by one objective ranking, or whether “natural” is vague or reflects human purposes more than philosophers sometimes admit.
key_ideas: Naturalness is a technical philosophical idea, not simply the opposite of “human-made” or “artificial.”
It is usually thought to come in degrees, and some theories include perfectly natural properties at the top.
Natural properties are supposed to be objective, although philosophers disagree about whether such a ranking exists.
The idea may help explain why some things seem similar, why some descriptions are basic, and why some words refer more easily than others.
Philosophers have connected naturalness with scientific laws and with learning from evidence, such as preferring “green” to “grue.”
There may be different kinds of naturalness for properties, classes, concepts, magnitudes, and natural kinds.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic connects a basic question about reality with practical questions about science and thinking. If some patterns are genuinely more fundamental, they might guide explanation, classification, language, and prediction. If not, we may need to explain why certain patterns feel better without saying that the world itself contains its own preferred divisions. Either way, the debate encourages careful thinking about simplicity, evidence, and the limits of our concepts.

important_terms.definition: A feature or relation that something can have, such as being green, triangular, or next to something.
The idea that some properties are less arbitrary and fit the world's structure better than others.
A property with the greatest possible degree of naturalness in a theory; it is also called fundamental.
A complicated property formed by joining conditions in an unusual way, often for a particular purpose.
A relation in which objects match in their basic, internal features, even if their surroundings differ.
The idea that one set of facts depends on another set without changing when the underlying facts stay fixed.
A property or relation that does not depend on what is outside the thing that has it.
A kind or category thought to reflect an important pattern in reality, such as a scientific kind; its relation to natural properties is debated.

questions_to_think_about: Is a rule involving a special date less natural because it is complicated, or only because it is less useful to us?
Would a perfectly natural property be easy to recognize?
Can two different properties have exactly the same examples but differ in naturalness?
Why might naturalness matter when scientists choose laws or generalizations?
Should “natural kind” mean the same thing as “natural property”?
